claims.text: Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in its simple solid-solution state has relatively low hardness and strength together with good ductility and machinability.
The mechanical-property combination of coarse-grained CoCrFeNiTi is governed by a dislocation-dominated microstructure with relatively few grain-boundary obstacles.
Other high-entropy alloys with high hardness and brittle behavior are strengthened by nanoscale grain-boundary and precipitate effects.
Grain refinement in CoCrFeNiTi should change the dominant deformation mechanism from dislocation glide to grain-boundary-mediated resistance.
Grain refinement should increase the hardness and strength of CoCrFeNiTi while reducing its ductility.
The starting material is equimolar CoCrFeNiTi with a relatively coarse-grained, simple solid-solution structure.
Severe plastic deformation and/or controlled heat treatment can produce nanoscale or sub-micron grains in CoCrFeNiTi without introducing secondary phases.
Thermally activated processes may intervene at temperatures around or above 600 °C.
The intervention will alter grain size, grain-boundary area, dislocation density, and the relative contributions of grain-boundary strengthening and dislocation-mediated plasticity.
In coarse-grained CoCrFeNiTi, dislocation glide accommodates plastic deformation and thereby promotes ductility while limiting strengthening.
Increasing grain-boundary area through grain refinement will impede dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion will increase hardness and compressive strength.
Nanocrystalline CoCrFeNiTi will have significantly greater hardness and compressive strength than the as-cast alloy.
Nanocrystalline CoCrFeNiTi will have lower ductility than the as-cast alloy.
The refined alloy should mechanically resemble high-entropy alloys that are brittle at room or elevated temperature because of grain-boundary and possible precipitate strengthening.

The proposed mechanism is limited to approximately equimolar, single-solid-solution CoCrFeNiTi without intentional grain-boundary phases or precipitates, under quasi-static loading from room temperature to about 600 °C.
